query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a two-step thermomechanical procedure (cryogenic rolling followed by short-duration, intermediate-temperature annealing) to as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy lamellar colonies will refine the dual-phase lamellae and partially recrystallize the structure, thereby improving both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility compared to the as-cast lamellar baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with a dual-phase lamellar microstructure (fcc/B2 or similar phases).
generation.intervention: Perform severe cryogenic rolling to introduce dense dislocations, followed by brief annealing at an intermediate temperature to promote partial recrystallization and hierarchical lamella refinement.
generation.structural_mediator: A partially recrystallized, hierarchically refined lamellar microstructure with stabilized phase boundaries and refined grain sizes.
generation.mechanism: During partial recrystallization, dislocations rearrange to form sub-boundaries and ultrafine grains, diminishing stress concentration sites and impeding microcrack initiation and propagation while maintaining high phase-interface strengthening.
generation.predicted_outcome: Yield strength and ultimate tensile strength each increase by at least 20–40% over the baseline. Total elongation at fracture is maintained or slightly improved (by up to ~25% or more), demonstrating a net gain in strength–ductility synergy versus as-cast lamellar colonies.
generation.baseline: Unmodified, as-cast EHEA lamellar colonies lacking sub-grain refinement, displaying limited room-temperature ductility and susceptibility to microcracking at colony boundaries.
generation.boundary: Over-annealing or insufficient cryorolling may fail to achieve the needed substructure refinement and can degrade strength or ductility via grain coarsening; excessively low annealing temperature or time may result in incomplete recrystallization, limiting ductility improvements.
generation.uncertainty: Optimal parameters (strain level, annealing temperature/time) require calibration for each alloy composition and may vary among eutectic high-entropy systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of samples with varying cryo-rolling reductions (e.g., 30%, 50%, 70%) and anneal them at different intermediate temperatures for controlled durations. Conduct uniaxial tensile tests at room temperature, followed by fractography and microstructural analyses to quantify crack initiation/propagation.
measurements: Yield and ultimate tensile strengths under tension
Microstructure (grain size, lamellar spacing, boundary characteristics)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no combination of cryo-rolling and annealing parameters yields improvements in both strength and ductility (i.e., if ductility fails to improve or if strength is not enhanced compared to the as-cast baseline), or if microcracking remains as prevalent as in the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Nano-lamellar (L12 + B2) AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (EHEA) was processed by cryo-rolling and annealing. The EHEA developed a novel hierarchical microstructure featured by fine lamellar regions consisting of FCC lamellae filled with ultrafine FCC grains (average size ~200–250 nm) and B2 lamellae, and coarse non-lamellar regions consisting of ultrafine FCC (average size ~200–250 nm), few coarse recrystallized FCC grains and rather coarse unrecrystallized B2 phase (~2.5 µm). This complex and hierarchical microstructure originated from differences in strain-partitioning amongst the constituent phases, affecting the driving force for recrystallization. The hierarchical microstructure of the cryo-rolled and annealed material resulted in simultaneous enhancement in strength (Yield Strength/YS: 1437 ± 26 MPa, Ultimate Tensile Strength/UTS: 1562 ± 33 MPa) and ductility (elongation to failure/ef ~ 14 ± 1%) as compared to the as-cast as well as cold-rolled and annealed materials. The room-temperature strength of Al0.3CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys (HEAs) is relatively low owing to its intrinsic fcc structure. In the present study, the as-cast HEAs were subjected to cold rolling and subsequent annealing treatment (800, 900, and 1000 °C) to adjust the microstructures and tensile properties. This treatment process resulted in the partial recrystallization, full recrystallization, and grain coarsening with increasing the annealing temperature. It was found that the large and spherical B2 precipitates were generated in the recrystallized grain boundaries of three annealing states, while the small and elongated B2 precipitates were aligned along the deformation twins in the non-recrystallized region of the 800 °C-annealing state. The former B2 precipitates assisted in refining the recrystallized grains to quasi ultra-fine grain and fine grain regimes (with the grain sizes of ~0.9, ~2.2, and ~7.2 μm). The tensile results indicated that the decreased annealing temperature induced the gradual strengthening of this alloy but also maintained the ductility at the high levels. decision.trend: Early work introduced AlCoCrFeNi-based eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs) with lamellar fcc/B2 or L12/B2 microstructures providing good strength, but often exhibiting limited ductility at room temperature. Subsequent studies showed that advanced thermomechanical routes—especially cryo-rolling and partial annealing—can introduce hierarchical or ultrafine lamellar structures, yielding improved strength–ductility synergy. Nevertheless, microcracking along phase boundaries and room-temperature brittleness remain critical, unresolved challenges, despite attempts to refine lamellae, promote twinning, or invert the matrix and precipitate phases. Further improvements require structural modifications that suppress premature fracture while preserving the dual-phase nature that confers high strength.
decision.unsolved: Microcracking initiates at interphase boundaries in the lamellar colonies and leads to catastrophic failure under room-temperature loading, indicating that more robust boundary modifications and tailored lamella architectures are needed to concurrently elevate both strength and ductility.
decision.lever: Apply a two-step deformation-and-annealing schedule—including cryogenic rolling to introduce dense dislocations, followed by short-duration, intermediate-temperature annealing to partially recrystallize and refine the lamellar colony structure—thereby creating a hierarchical microstructure that impedes crack propagation while retaining high strength.
decision.why: Prior studies (e.g., cryo-rolling + annealing) demonstrate that partial recrystallization and sub-lamellar refinement can effectively hinder microcrack initiation and provide strengthened interfaces. This enabled hierarchical fcc/B2 lamellae with reduced boundary stress concentrations, thus promising improved tensile ductility alongside high strength at room temperature. The testable hypothesis is that the resulting hierarchical lamellar microstructure will both raise yield strength (due to refined grain and lamellar spacing) and enhance fracture resistance (by distributing strain and deflecting cracks). By varying the extent of cryo-rolling and annealing temperature/time, one can test whether a continuous transition from lamellar to semi-equiaxed grains correlates with increasing ductility. A critical test for falsification is to measure fracture strain in uniaxial tension at room temperature across different annealing protocols: if microcracking is not reduced and ductility does not improve relative to the baseline as-cast lamellar condition, this would refute the hypothesis.
